title: Bruder Lustig
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 1, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 81. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 81, the longest of the soldier tales, and the one that lets a scoundrel into heaven anyway. A discharged soldier gives his bread and his last kreuzers to three beggars who are all Saint Peter, then travels with the apostle, who raises the dead by cutting them up, washing the bones and calling them back to life. Brother Lustig eats the lamb’s heart and denies it through rising water, tries the miracle himself for money and makes butchery of it, and is bailed out; at parting Peter gives his knapsack the power that whatever he wishes into it is there — which is how, in the end, he gets past the gate. Spelling follows the 1857 edition (gieng, fieng, thun, Thür, todt, ward, Commißbrot).

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein großer Krieg, und als der Krieg zu Ende war, bekamen viele Soldaten ihren Abschied.
sentences.l: There was once a great war, and when the war was at an end, many soldiers received their discharge.
sentences.i: Once there was a great war, and when the war came to an end, many soldiers were discharged.
sentences.n: Es war einmal is the fixed opening of a German tale — literally “it was once,” our “once upon a time.” seinen Abschied bekommen is the set phrase for being let go from military service.

sentences.t: Nun bekam der Bruder Lustig auch seinen Abschied und sonst nichts als ein kleines Laibchen Commißbrot und vier Kreuzer an Geld; damit zog er fort.
sentences.l: Now Brother Lustig too received his discharge and nothing else than a little loaf of ration-bread and four Kreuzer in money; with that he moved off.
sentences.i: Now Brother Lustig got his discharge as well, and nothing besides a small loaf of army bread and four kreuzers in money; with that he set off.
sentences.n: Lustig means merry, so his name is something like Brother Merry; it is left standing as a name. Commißbrot is the coarse ration bread issued to soldiers, and a Kreuzer is a small copper coin, so four of them are next to nothing. Laibchen is the diminutive of Laib, a loaf.

sentences.t: Der heilige Petrus aber hatte sich als ein armer Bettler an den Weg gesetzt, und wie der Bruder Lustig daher kam, bat er ihn um ein Almosen.
sentences.l: Saint Peter, however, had seated himself as a poor beggar by the way, and as Brother Lustig came along, he asked him for an alms.
sentences.i: But Saint Peter had sat down by the roadside as a poor beggar, and when Brother Lustig came along, he begged an alms of him.
sentences.n: sich setzen is reflexive — literally “had set himself” — where English simply says sat down. wie here means “when,” not “how”; you will meet it constantly in the tales.

sentences.t: Er antwortete „lieber Bettelmann, was soll ich dir geben?
sentences.l: He answered “dear beggarman, what am I to give you?
sentences.i: He answered, “My good beggarman, what am I supposed to give you?
sentences.n: soll is not moral obligation here but “am I to,” asking what is expected of him; dir is the dative of the person given to. The speech runs on through the next two units, so the closing quotation mark does not come until the end of it.

sentences.t: ich bin Soldat gewesen und habe meinen Abschied bekommen, und habe sonst nichts als das kleine Commißbrot und vier Kreuzer Geld, wenn das all ist, muß ich betteln, so gut wie du.
sentences.l: I have been a soldier and have received my discharge, and have nothing else than the little ration-bread and four Kreuzer of money; when that is all [gone], I must beg, just as well as you.
sentences.i: I have been a soldier and have taken my discharge, and I have nothing but the small loaf of army bread and four kreuzers in money; when that is used up I must beg, just as you do.
sentences.n: all is the colloquial alle, “used up, gone” — wenn das all ist means “when that is finished,” not “when that is everything”; the literal supplies [gone] in brackets because English cannot use all that way. Note also that a German predicate noun takes no article: ich bin Soldat gewesen.

sentences.t: Doch geben will ich dir was.“
sentences.l: Still, give you something I will.”
sentences.i: But I will give you something.”
sentences.n: Doch geben will ich dir was — the infinitive geben is thrown to the front for emphasis, which leaves the finite verb will in second place and the subject after it; English can only echo the shape by inverting.

sentences.t: Darauf theilte er den Laib in vier Theile, und gab davon dem Apostel einen und auch einen Kreuzer.
sentences.l: Thereupon he divided the loaf into four parts, and gave of them to the apostle one and also a Kreuzer.
sentences.i: Thereupon he divided the loaf into four parts and gave the apostle one of them, and a kreuzer with it.
sentences.n: theilte and Theile are the 1857 spellings of teilte and Teile. davon … einen means “one of them,” the davon pointing back to the four parts.

sentences.t: Der heilige Petrus bedankte sich, gieng weiter und setzte sich in einer andern Gestalt wieder als Bettelmann dem Soldaten an den Weg, und als er zu ihm kam, bat er ihn, wie das vorigemal, um eine Gabe.
sentences.l: Saint Peter thanked him, went further and set himself in another shape again as a beggarman by the soldier’s way, and when he came to him, he asked him, as the previous time, for a gift.
sentences.i: Saint Peter thanked him, went on, and in another shape sat down again as a beggarman in the soldier’s path, and when the soldier came up he asked him, as before, for a gift.
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging. sich bedanken is reflexive, “to give thanks.” dem Soldaten an den Weg is a dative of the person concerned — “in the soldier’s way” — the dative doing the work of an English possessive.

sentences.t: Der Bruder Lustig sprach wie vorher und gab ihm wieder ein Viertel von dem Brot und einen Kreuzer.
sentences.l: Brother Lustig spoke as before and gave him again a quarter of the bread and a Kreuzer.
sentences.n: sprach is the old narrative past of sprechen, “said”; the tales use it where modern German would use sagte.

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus bedankte sich und gieng weiter, setzte sich aber zum drittenmal in einer andern Gestalt als ein Bettler an den Weg und sprach den Bruder Lustig an.
sentences.l: Saint Peter thanked him and went further, but set himself for the third time in another shape as a beggar by the way and spoke to Brother Lustig.
sentences.i: Saint Peter thanked him and went on, but for the third time he sat down by the road in another shape as a beggar and addressed Brother Lustig.
sentences.n: heil. is the printed abbreviation of heilig, “holy, saint.” ansprechen is a separable verb, so its prefix an drops to the end of the clause: sprach … an, “addressed.”

sentences.t: Der Bruder Lustig gab ihm auch das dritte Viertel Brot und den dritten Kreuzer.
sentences.l: Brother Lustig gave him the third quarter of bread and the third Kreuzer too.
sentences.i: Brother Lustig gave him the third quarter of the loaf and the third kreuzer as well.

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus bedankte sich, und der Bruder Lustig gieng weiter und hatte nicht mehr als ein Viertel Brot und einen Kreuzer.
sentences.l: Saint Peter thanked him, and Brother Lustig went further and had no more than a quarter of bread and one Kreuzer.
sentences.i: Saint Peter thanked him, and Brother Lustig went on his way with no more than a quarter of the loaf and a single kreuzer.
sentences.n: The soldier has now given away three quarters of everything he owns, and the tale counts the gifts out one by one, in the threefold rhythm these tales like.

sentences.t: Damit gieng er in ein Wirthshaus, aß das Brot und ließ sich für den Kreuzer Bier dazu geben.
sentences.l: With that he went into an inn, ate the bread and had beer given to himself for the Kreuzer with it.
sentences.i: With that he went into an inn, ate the bread, and had beer served with it for his kreuzer.
sentences.n: sich etwas geben lassen — lassen with an infinitive means “to have something done,” and the reflexive sich says it is done for him. Wirthshaus is the 1857 spelling of Wirtshaus, an inn.

sentences.t: Als er fertig war, zog er weiter, und da gieng ihm der heil. Petrus gleichfalls in der Gestalt eines verabschiedeten Soldaten entgegen und redete ihn an, „guten Tag, Camerad, kannst du mir nicht ein Stück Brot geben und einen Kreuzer zu einem Trunk?“
sentences.l: When he was finished, he moved further on, and there Saint Peter came toward him likewise in the shape of a discharged soldier and addressed him, “good day, comrade, can you not give me a piece of bread and a Kreuzer for a drink?”
sentences.i: When he had finished he moved on, and there Saint Peter came to meet him, this time in the shape of a discharged soldier, and addressed him: “Good day, comrade, can you not spare me a piece of bread and a kreuzer for a drink?”
sentences.n: entgegengehen is separable and takes the dative: gieng ihm … entgegen, “went to meet him.” Camerad is the 1857 spelling of Kamerad.

sentences.t: „Wo soll ichs hernehmen,“ antwortete der Bruder Lustig, „ich habe meinen Abschied und sonst nichts als einen Laib Commißbrot und vier Kreuzer an Geld bekommen.
sentences.l: “Where am I to take it from,” answered Brother Lustig, “I have received my discharge and nothing else than a loaf of ration-bread and four Kreuzer in money.
sentences.i: “Where should I get it from?” answered Brother Lustig. “I got my discharge and nothing besides a loaf of army bread and four kreuzers in money.
sentences.n: hernehmen is separable, “to take from somewhere,” and wo … hernehmen is the idiom for “where am I supposed to find it.” ichs is ich es run together, as the words sound in speech.

sentences.t: Drei Bettler sind mir auf der Landstraße begegnet, davon hab ich jedem ein Viertel von meinem Brot und einen Kreuzer Geld gegeben.
sentences.l: Three beggars have met me on the highroad, of them I have given each a quarter of my bread and a Kreuzer of money.
sentences.i: Three beggars met me on the highroad, and I gave each of them a quarter of my bread and a kreuzer.
sentences.n: begegnen takes the dative — mir begegnet, “met me” — and builds its perfect with sein rather than haben.

sentences.t: Das letzte Viertel hab ich im Wirthshaus gegessen und für den letzten Kreuzer dazu getrunken.
sentences.l: The last quarter I have eaten in the inn and for the last Kreuzer drunk with it.
sentences.i: The last quarter I ate at the inn, and drank the last kreuzer away with it.
sentences.n: The object Das letzte Viertel stands first for emphasis, which pushes hab into second place — German’s rule is not subject-first but verb-second.

sentences.t: Jetzt bin ich leer, und wenn du auch nichts mehr hast, so können wir mit einander betteln gehen.“
sentences.l: Now I am empty, and if you also have nothing more, then we can go begging with one another.”
sentences.i: Now I am cleaned out, and if you have nothing left either, then the two of us can go begging together.”
sentences.n: leer sein is said of a purse and of a man. betteln gehen puts a bare infinitive with gehen, “to go and beg,” like einkaufen gehen.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der heil. Petrus, „das wird just nicht nöthig sein: ich verstehe mich ein wenig auf die Doctorei, und damit will ich mir schon so viel verdienen als ich brauche.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered Saint Peter, “that will precisely not be necessary: I understand myself a little on doctoring, and with that I will earn myself as much as I need, never fear.”
sentences.i: “No,” answered Saint Peter, “there will be no need of that: I know a little about doctoring, and with it I shall earn myself as much as I need.”
sentences.n: sich verstehen auf etwas is the fixed idiom for being skilled in something; the reflexive cannot be translated on its own. schon in a promise means “sure enough, never fear,” not “already.” nöthig is the 1857 nötig. just here is the older adverb “precisely,” and is not the English “just.”

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sagte der Bruder Lustig, „davon verstehe ich nichts, also muß ich allein betteln gehen.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” said Brother Lustig, “of that I understand nothing, so I must go begging alone.”
sentences.i: “Well,” said Brother Lustig, “I know nothing of that, so I must go begging on my own.”
sentences.n: davon verstehe ich nichts is the everyday way of saying “that is not my line.” The fronted davon again pushes the verb into second place.

sentences.t: „Nun komm nur mit,“ sprach der heil. Petrus, „wenn ich was verdiene, sollst du die Hälfte davon haben.“
sentences.l: “Now just come along,” said Saint Peter, “if I earn something, you shall have the half of it.”
sentences.i: “Come along with me,” said Saint Peter, “if I earn anything you shall have half of it.”
sentences.n: mitkommen is separable: komm … mit. nur with an imperative softens it to “just, do.” was is the shortened etwas.

sentences.t: „Das ist mir wohl recht“ sagte der Bruder Lustig.
sentences.l: “That is well right to me,” said Brother Lustig.
sentences.i: “That suits me well enough,” said Brother Lustig.
sentences.n: mir recht sein — dative plus recht — is the set phrase for “to be all right with me.” The 1857 print gives no comma before sagte here; it stands as printed.

sentences.t: Also zogen sie mit einander fort.
sentences.l: So moved they forth with one another.
sentences.i: So the two of them went off together.

sentences.t: Nun kamen sie an ein Bauernhaus und hörten darin gewaltig jammern und schreien, da giengen sie hinein, so lag der Mann darin auf den Tod krank und war nah am Verscheiden, und die Frau heulte und weinte ganz laut.
sentences.l: Now they came to a farmhouse and heard inside it mighty wailing and shrieking; so they went in, and there the man lay inside sick unto death and was near to expiring, and the woman howled and wept quite loudly.
sentences.i: Now they came to a farmhouse and heard a great wailing and crying inside, so they went in, and there lay the husband, sick to death and close to breathing his last, while his wife howled and wept aloud.
sentences.n: hörten … jammern und schreien uses a bare infinitive after a verb of perception, like English “heard them wailing.” auf den Tod krank is the old phrase for sick unto death, and Verscheiden, an infinitive used as a noun, is the gentle word for dying.

sentences.t: „Laßt euer Heulen und Weinen,“ sprach der heil. Petrus, „ich will den Mann wieder gesund machen,“ nahm eine Salbe aus der Tasche und heilte den Kranken augenblicklich, so daß er aufstehen konnte, und ganz gesund war.
sentences.l: “Leave off your howling and weeping,” said Saint Peter, “I will make the man healthy again,” took a salve out of the pocket and healed the sick man in a moment, so that he could get up and was quite well.
sentences.i: “Leave off your howling and weeping,” said Saint Peter, “I will make the man well again,” and he took a salve out of his pocket and healed the sick man on the spot, so that he could get up and was quite sound.
sentences.n: Laßt is the plural imperative, addressed to the household. gesund machen, “to make well,” is the tale’s standing phrase for healing, and den Kranken is an adjective used as a noun, “the sick one.” The narration runs straight on out of the speech without naming the subject again.

sentences.t: Sprachen Mann und Frau in großer Freude „wie können wir euch lohnen? was sollen wir euch geben?“
sentences.l: Spoke man and wife in great joy “how can we reward you? what are we to give you?”
sentences.i: The man and his wife said in great joy, “How can we reward you? What are we to give you?”
sentences.n: The sentence opens with its verb, Sprachen — a lively narrative inversion the tales use constantly, where English needs a subject first. euch is the plural you addressed to the two travellers.

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus aber wollte nichts nehmen, und jemehr ihn die Bauersleute baten, desto mehr weigerte er sich.
sentences.l: Saint Peter, however, would take nothing, and the more the farm-folk begged him, the more he refused.
sentences.i: But Saint Peter would take nothing, and the more the farming couple pressed him, the more he refused.
sentences.n: jemehr … desto mehr is the German “the more … the more”; jemehr is printed as one word here, today je mehr. sich weigern is reflexive, “to refuse.”

sentences.t: Der Bruder Lustig aber stieß den heil. Petrus an, und sagte „so nimm doch was, wir brauchens ja.“
sentences.l: Brother Lustig, however, nudged Saint Peter, and said “do take something, we need it after all.”
sentences.i: But Brother Lustig gave Saint Peter a nudge and said, “Do take something — we need it, do we not.”
sentences.n: anstoßen is separable, “to nudge.” doch presses a command: “do take.” ja tucked into a sentence appeals to what both parties already know. brauchens is brauchen es run together.

sentences.t: Endlich brachte die Bäuerin ein Lamm und sprach zu dem heil. Petrus das müßte er annehmen, aber er wollte es nicht.
sentences.l: At last the farmwife brought a lamb and said to Saint Peter he must accept it, but he would not.
sentences.i: At last the farmer’s wife brought a lamb and told Saint Peter that he really must accept it, but he would not.
sentences.n: das müßte er annehmen is reported speech: the subjunctive müßte marks the words as hers rather than the narrator’s, and German reports with no “that” at all. The ß in müßte is regular 1857 spelling.

sentences.t: Da stieß ihn der Bruder Lustig in die Seite und sprach „nimms doch, dummer Teufel, wir brauchens ja.“
sentences.l: Then Brother Lustig poked him in the side and said “take it, you stupid devil, we need it after all.”
sentences.i: Then Brother Lustig jabbed him in the ribs and said, “Take it, you stupid devil, we need it.”
sentences.n: in die Seite with the accusative, because the poke moves into it. nimms is nimm es. The abuse of a saint is in the text and stands.

sentences.t: Da sagte der heil. Petrus endlich „ja, das Lamm will ich nehmen, aber ich trags nicht: wenn dus willst, so mußt du es tragen.“
sentences.l: Then said Saint Peter at last “yes, the lamb I will take, but I carry it not: if you want it, then you must carry it.”
sentences.i: Then Saint Peter said at last, “Very well, I will take the lamb, but I am not carrying it: if you want it, you must carry it yourself.”
sentences.n: das Lamm is fronted for contrast, with the verb still second. trags and dus are trag es and du es run together — the tales print speech as it sounds.

sentences.t: „Das hat keine Noth,“ sprach der Bruder Lustig, „das will ich schon tragen,“ und nahms auf die Schulter.
sentences.l: “That has no need,” said Brother Lustig, “that I will carry sure enough,” and took it on the shoulder.
sentences.i: “No trouble at all,” said Brother Lustig, “I will carry it, never fear,” and he took it on his shoulder.
sentences.n: das hat keine Noth is the old idiom “there is no difficulty in that, never mind.” Noth is the 1857 Not, and schon again means “never fear.” nahms is nahm es.

sentences.t: Nun giengen sie fort und kamen in einen Wald, da war das Lamm dem Bruder Lustig schwer geworden, er aber war hungrig, also sprach er zu dem heil. Petrus „schau, da ist ein schöner Platz, da könnten wir das Lamm kochen und verzehren.“
sentences.l: Now they went off and came into a wood; there the lamb had grown heavy to Brother Lustig, but he was hungry, so he said to Saint Peter “look, there is a fine spot, there we could cook the lamb and consume it.”
sentences.i: Now they went on and came into a wood; by then the lamb had grown heavy for Brother Lustig, and he was hungry besides, so he said to Saint Peter, “Look, there is a fine spot — we could cook the lamb here and eat it.”
sentences.n: dem Bruder Lustig is a dative of the person affected: the lamb had grown heavy for him. verzehren is the elevated word for eating up, kept as “consume” in the literal.

sentences.t: „Mir ists recht,“ antwortete der heil. Petrus, „doch kann ich mit der Kocherei nicht umgehen: willst du kochen, so hast du da einen Kessel, ich will derweil auf und ab gehen, bis es gahr ist.
sentences.l: “It is right to me,” answered Saint Peter, “yet with the cookery I cannot deal: will you cook, then you have a kettle there, I will meanwhile go up and down, until it is done.
sentences.i: “That suits me,” answered Saint Peter, “only I am no hand at cooking: if you will do the cooking, there is a kettle for you, and I will walk up and down meanwhile until it is done.
sentences.n: mit etwas umgehen means to handle or manage something. The ending -erei in Kocherei has a faintly dismissive ring, “the whole business of cooking.” willst du kochen, with the verb first and no wenn, is a conditional: “if you will cook.” gahr is the 1857 gar, cooked through.

sentences.t: Du mußt aber nicht eher zu essen anfangen, als bis ich wieder zurück bin; ich will schon zu rechter Zeit kommen.“
sentences.l: You must, however, not sooner begin to eat than until I am back again; I will come at the right time, never fear.”
sentences.i: But you must not begin eating before I am back again; I shall come at the right moment, never fear.”
sentences.n: nicht eher … als bis is the frame “not before … until.” anfangen is separable and takes zu with the infinitive, so zu essen stands before the verb that carries the prefix.

sentences.t: „Geh nur,“ sagte Bruder Lustig, „ich verstehe mich aufs Kochen, ich wills schon machen.“
sentences.l: “Just go,” said Brother Lustig, “I understand myself on the cooking, I will manage it sure enough.”
sentences.i: “Off you go,” said Brother Lustig, “cooking is something I know about, I shall manage it.”
sentences.n: sich verstehen auf again, this time with aufs = auf das and the infinitive Kochen used as a noun. wills is will es.

sentences.t: Da gieng der heil. Petrus fort, und der Bruder Lustig schlachtete das Lamm, machte Feuer an, warf das Fleisch in den Kessel und kochte.
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter went off, and Brother Lustig slaughtered the lamb, made a fire, threw the flesh into the kettle and cooked.
sentences.i: Then Saint Peter went off, and Brother Lustig slaughtered the lamb, lit a fire, threw the meat into the kettle and cooked it.
sentences.n: Feuer anmachen, separable, is the ordinary phrase for lighting a fire. kochte stands with no object in German where English wants “cooked it.”

sentences.t: Das Lamm war aber schon gahr und der Apostel noch immer nicht zurück, da nahm es der Bruder Lustig aus dem Kessel, zerschnitt es und fand das Herz.
sentences.l: The lamb, however, was already done and the apostle still not back, so Brother Lustig took it out of the kettle, cut it up and found the heart.
sentences.i: But the lamb was done already and the apostle still not back, so Brother Lustig took it out of the kettle, cut it up, and found the heart.
sentences.n: The second clause has no verb of its own — und der Apostel noch immer nicht zurück leaves war to be carried over from the first, which German does easily.

sentences.t: „Das soll das Beste sein,“ sprach er und versuchte es, zuletzt aber aß er es ganz auf.
sentences.l: “That is supposed to be the best,” said he and tasted it, at last however he ate it quite up.
sentences.i: “That is said to be the best part,” he said, and he tasted it — and in the end he ate the whole of it.
sentences.n: sollen with an infinitive can report hearsay, “it is said to be.” versuchen here has its older sense of tasting, sampling, not trying. aufessen is separable, “to eat up.”

sentences.t: Endlich kam der heil. Petrus zurück und sprach „du kannst das ganze Lamm allein essen, ich will nur das Herz davon, das gib mir.“
sentences.l: At last Saint Peter came back and said “you can eat the whole lamb alone, I want only the heart of it, that give me.”
sentences.i: At last Saint Peter came back and said, “You may eat the whole lamb by yourself, I want only the heart of it — give me that.”
sentences.n: das gib mir puts the object first and then leaves it standing before the imperative, a plain spoken emphasis German allows freely.

sentences.t: Da nahm Bruder Lustig Messer und Gabel, that als suchte er eifrig in dem Lammfleisch herum, konnte aber das Herz nicht finden;
sentences.l: Then Brother Lustig took knife and fork, did as if he searched eagerly about in the lamb’s flesh, but could not find the heart;
sentences.i: Then Brother Lustig took up knife and fork and made as though he were rummaging eagerly through the lamb’s flesh, but he could not find the heart;
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat, from thun (tun). thun als … is the idiom “to act as though,” and after als the verb follows straight away: suchte er. herumsuchen is separable.

sentences.t: endlich sagte er kurz weg „es ist keins da.“
sentences.l: at last he said short off “there is none there.”
sentences.i: at last he said flatly, “There is none.”
sentences.n: kurz weg, today kurzweg, means bluntly, without more ado. keins is keines, standing for kein Herz.

sentences.t: „Nun, wo solls denn sein?“ sagte der Apostel.
sentences.l: “Now, where is it supposed to be then?” said the apostle.
sentences.i: “Well then, where can it be?” said the apostle.
sentences.n: denn inside a question is not the conjunction “for” but the little word of impatience or curiosity, “then, I wonder.” solls is soll es.

sentences.t: „Das weiß ich nicht,“ antwortete der Bruder Lustig, „aber schau, was sind wir alle beide für Narren, suchen das Herz vom Lamm und fällt keinem von uns ein, ein Lamm hat ja kein Herz!“
sentences.l: “That I do not know,” answered Brother Lustig, “but look, what fools are we both, we search the heart of the lamb and it occurs to neither of us, a lamb has no heart, after all!”
sentences.i: “I do not know,” answered Brother Lustig, “but look here, what a pair of fools we are, hunting for the lamb’s heart, and it never occurs to either of us that a lamb has no heart!”
sentences.n: was … für Narren is the frame “what sort of fools”; für does not mean “for” here. einfallen is separable and takes the dative of the person — fällt keinem von uns ein, “it strikes neither of us.” The final clause is what does not strike them, joined without daß.

sentences.t: „Ei,“ sprach der heil. Petrus, „das ist was ganz Neues, jedes Thier hat ja ein Herz, warum sollt ein Lamm kein Herz haben?“
sentences.l: “Why,” said Saint Peter, “that is something quite new, every animal has a heart, to be sure, why should a lamb have no heart?”
sentences.i: “Well now,” said Saint Peter, “that is news to me; every animal has a heart, surely — why should a lamb have none?”
sentences.n: Thier is the 1857 Tier. was ganz Neues is etwas ganz Neues, with the adjective turned into a noun. sollt is the clipped sollte.

sentences.t: „Nein, gewißlich, Bruder, ein Lamm hat kein Herz, denk nur recht nach, so wird dirs einfallen, es hat im Ernst keins.“
sentences.l: “No, certainly, brother, a lamb has no heart, only think it properly over, then it will occur to you, it has in earnest none.”
sentences.i: “No, truly, brother, a lamb has no heart; only think it over properly and it will come to you — it really has none.”
sentences.n: nachdenken is separable: denk … nach, “think it over.” dirs is dir es, with einfallen once more taking the dative. im Ernst, “in earnest, seriously.”

sentences.t: „Nun, es ist schon gut,“ sagte der heil. Petrus, „ist kein Herz da, so brauch ich auch nichts vom Lamm, du kannsts allein essen.“
sentences.l: “Now, it is all right,” said Saint Peter, “is there no heart there, then I need nothing of the lamb either, you can eat it alone.”
sentences.i: “Well, let it be,” said Saint Peter, “if there is no heart, then I want none of the lamb either — you may eat it by yourself.”
sentences.n: ist kein Herz da is again a conditional made by putting the verb first, “if there is no heart.” kannsts is kannst es, and es ist schon gut means “never mind, let it be.”

sentences.t: „Was ich halt nicht aufessen kann, das nehm ich mit in meinem Ranzen“ sprach der Bruder Lustig, aß das halbe Lamm und steckte das übrige in seinen Ranzen.
sentences.l: “What I just cannot eat up, that I take along in my knapsack,” said Brother Lustig, ate the half lamb and put the rest into his knapsack.
sentences.i: “Whatever I cannot finish I take along in my knapsack,” said Brother Lustig, and he ate half the lamb and stowed the rest in his knapsack.
sentences.n: halt is the southern particle of resignation, “just, simply.” The clause Was ich … kann is then picked up by das, a doubling German likes when a whole clause is the object. A Ranzen is a soldier’s pack, and it will carry the rest of the tale.

sentences.t: Sie giengen weiter, da machte der heil. Petrus daß ein großes Wasser queer über den Weg floß und sie hindurch mußten.
sentences.l: They went further; then Saint Peter brought it about that a great water flowed crosswise over the way and they had to [go] through.
sentences.i: They went on, and then Saint Peter made a great stretch of water flow across the path so that they had to go through it.
sentences.n: machen daß, “to bring it about that.” queer is the 1857 quer, crosswise. sie hindurch mußten has no verb of motion at all — müssen carries it alone — so the literal supplies [go] in brackets.

sentences.t: Sprach der heil. Petrus „geh du nur voran.“
sentences.l: Said Saint Peter “just go you in front.”
sentences.i: Saint Peter said, “You go on ahead.”
sentences.n: The pronoun du is added to the imperative geh for emphasis — you and not I. vorangehen is separable.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der Bruder Lustig, „geh du voran,“ und dachte „wenn dem das Wasser zu tief ist, so bleib ich zurück.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered Brother Lustig, “you go in front,” and thought “if the water is too deep for that one, then I stay back.”
sentences.i: “No,” answered Brother Lustig, “you go ahead,” and he thought, “If the water is too deep for him, then I shall stay behind.”
sentences.n: dem is the demonstrative der used of a person, a shade dismissive, “that fellow.” zu tief takes the dative of the one it is too deep for. Thoughts are quoted exactly like speech.

sentences.t: Da schritt der heil. Petrus hindurch, und das Wasser gieng ihm nur bis ans Knie.
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter strode through, and the water went to him only up to the knee.
sentences.i: Then Saint Peter strode through, and the water came only up to his knee.
sentences.n: ihm … bis ans Knie is the dative of possession: German says the water went to him up to the knee, English says up to his knee. ans is an das.

sentences.t: Nun wollte Bruder Lustig auch hindurch, aber das Wasser wurde größer und stieg ihm an den Hals.
sentences.l: Now Brother Lustig wanted through too, but the water became greater and rose to his neck.
sentences.i: Now Brother Lustig wanted to cross as well, but the water grew and rose to his neck.
sentences.n: wollte … hindurch again has no verb of motion; wollen carries it. The dative ihm is once more the possessive, “his neck.”

sentences.t: Da rief er „Bruder, hilf mir.“
sentences.l: Then he cried “brother, help me.”

sentences.t: Sagte der heil. Petrus „willst du auch gestehen daß du das Herz von dem Lamm gegessen hast?“
sentences.l: Said Saint Peter “will you now confess that you have eaten the heart of the lamb?”
sentences.i: Saint Peter said, “Will you confess now that you ate the lamb’s heart?”
sentences.n: auch in a question like this presses for an admission, roughly “now, really.” In the daß-clause the verb group goes to the end: gegessen hast.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete er, „ich hab es nicht gegessen.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered he, “I have not eaten it.”
sentences.i: “No,” he answered, “I did not eat it.”

sentences.t: Da ward das Wasser noch größer, und stieg ihm bis an den Mund: „hilf mir, Bruder,“ rief der Soldat.
sentences.l: Then the water became still greater, and rose to his mouth: “help me, brother,” cried the soldier.
sentences.i: Then the water grew greater still and rose to his mouth: “Help me, brother,” cried the soldier.
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, modern wurde — a form these tales use constantly. noch größer, “greater still.”

sentences.t: Sprach der heil. Petrus noch einmal „willst du auch gestehen daß du das Herz vom Lamm gegessen hast?“
sentences.l: Said Saint Peter once more “will you now confess that you have eaten the heart of the lamb?”
sentences.i: Saint Peter said once more, “Will you confess now that you ate the lamb’s heart?”
sentences.n: vom is von dem. The question comes back almost word for word: repetition with small variation is how the tale builds its pressure.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete er, „ich hab es nicht gegessen.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered he, “I have not eaten it.”
sentences.i: “No,” he answered, “I did not eat it.”

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus wollte ihn doch nicht ertrinken lassen, ließ das Wasser wieder fallen und half ihm hinüber.
sentences.l: Saint Peter would nevertheless not let him drown, let the water fall again and helped him over.
sentences.i: Still, Saint Peter would not let him drown; he let the water fall again and helped him across.
sentences.n: ertrinken lassen is lassen with a bare infinitive, “to let someone drown.” doch here means “all the same, for all that.”

sentences.t: Nun zogen sie weiter, und kamen in ein Reich, da hörten sie daß die Königstochter todtkrank läge.
sentences.l: Now they moved further, and came into a kingdom, where they heard that the king’s daughter lay sick unto death.
sentences.i: Now they went on and came into a kingdom, where they heard that the king’s daughter lay mortally ill.
sentences.n: läge is the subjunctive of liegen, marking the report as hearsay — what they heard, not what the tale asserts. todtkrank is the 1857 todkrank.

sentences.t: „Holla, Bruder,“ sprach der Soldat zum heil. Petrus, „da ist ein Fang für uns, wenn wir die gesund machen, so ist uns auf ewige Zeiten geholfen.“
sentences.l: “Hallo, brother,” said the soldier to Saint Peter, “there is a catch for us, if we make her well, then we are helped for eternal times.”
sentences.i: “Hallo there, brother,” said the soldier to Saint Peter, “here is a catch for us: if we make her well, we are provided for to the end of time.”
sentences.n: Fang is a fisherman’s or hunter’s catch — the soldier sees a haul, not a patient. uns ist geholfen is an impersonal passive with the dative, literally “to us it is helped,” i.e. we are provided for. die is the demonstrative standing for “her.”

sentences.t: Da war ihm der heil. Petrus nicht geschwind genug, „nun, heb die Beine auf, Bruderherz,“ sprach er zu ihm, „daß wir noch zu rechter Zeit hin kommen.“
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter was not quick enough for him: “now, lift the legs up, brother-heart,” said he to him, “that we come there still at the right time.”
sentences.i: Saint Peter was not quick enough for him: “Come, pick up your feet, brother dear,” he said to him, “so that we get there in time.”
sentences.n: ihm is again the dative of the person concerned, “for him.” die Beine takes the plain article where English says “your.” Bruderherz, literally brother-heart, is a coaxing address — the soldier flatters when he wants something. daß alone here means “so that.”

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus gieng aber immer langsamer, wie auch der Bruder Lustig ihn trieb und schob, bis sie endlich hörten die Königstochter wäre gestorben.
sentences.l: Saint Peter, however, went ever more slowly, however much Brother Lustig drove and shoved him, until they at last heard the king’s daughter had died.
sentences.i: But Saint Peter walked slower and slower, however much Brother Lustig urged and pushed him, until at last they heard that the king’s daughter had died.
sentences.n: immer with a comparative means “more and more.” wie auch … here is concessive, “however much.” wäre gestorben is once more the subjunctive of reported speech, and the daß is simply left out.

sentences.t: „Da haben wirs,“ sprach der Bruder Lustig, „das kommt von deinem schläfrigen Gang.“
sentences.l: “There have we it,” said Brother Lustig, “that comes of your sleepy gait.”
sentences.i: “There we have it,” said Brother Lustig, “that comes of your sleepy pace.”
sentences.n: wirs is wir es. kommen von means “to come of, be the result of.”

sentences.t: „Sei nur still,“ antwortete der heil. Petrus, „ich kann noch mehr als Kranke gesund machen, ich kann auch Todte wieder ins Leben erwecken.“
sentences.l: “Only be still,” answered Saint Peter, “I can do more than make sick people well, I can also wake the dead again into life.”
sentences.i: “Be quiet,” answered Saint Peter, “I can do more than make sick people well — I can wake the dead back into life.”
sentences.n: Kranke and Todte are adjectives used as nouns, “sick ones, dead ones”; Todte is the 1857 Tote. erwecken, to wake or rouse, is the word used of raising the dead.

sentences.t: „Nun, wenn das ist,“ sagte der Bruder Lustig, „so laß ich mirs gefallen, das halbe Königreich mußt du uns aber zum wenigsten damit verdienen.“
sentences.l: “Now, if that is [so],” said Brother Lustig, “then I let it please me; the half kingdom, however, you must earn us with it at the very least.”
sentences.i: “Well, if that is how it is,” said Brother Lustig, “then I am content; but you must earn us half the kingdom with it at the very least.”
sentences.n: sich etwas gefallen lassen is the fixed idiom for putting up with or being content with a thing; mirs is mir es. The German wenn das ist has no complement of its own, so the literal supplies [so] in brackets. zum wenigsten is the older form of wenigstens.

sentences.t: Darauf giengen sie in das königliche Schloß, wo alles in großer Trauer war: der heil. Petrus aber sagte zu dem König er wollte die Tochter wieder lebendig machen.
sentences.l: Thereupon they went into the royal castle, where everything was in great mourning: Saint Peter, however, said to the king he would make the daughter alive again.
sentences.i: Thereupon they went into the royal castle, where all was in deep mourning; but Saint Peter told the king that he would make his daughter live again.
sentences.n: er wollte die Tochter … is reported speech once more, the verb form alone marking it and no daß to introduce it.

sentences.t: Da ward er zu ihr geführt, und dann sprach er „bringt mir einen Kessel mit Wasser,“ und wie der gebracht war, hieß er jedermann hinausgehen, und nur der Bruder Lustig durfte bei ihm bleiben.
sentences.l: Then he was led to her, and then he said “bring me a kettle with water,” and when it was brought, he bade everyone go out, and only Brother Lustig was allowed to stay with him.
sentences.i: Then he was led to her, and he said, “Bring me a kettle of water,” and when it had been brought he bade everyone go out, and only Brother Lustig was allowed to stay with him.
sentences.n: ward … geführt is the passive with the old ward for wurde. heißen with a bare infinitive means to bid someone do a thing: hieß … hinausgehen. der stands for “it,” the kettle — the demonstrative doing pronoun duty.

sentences.t: Darauf schnitt er alle Glieder der Todten los und warf sie ins Wasser, machte Feuer unter den Kessel und ließ sie kochen.
sentences.l: Thereupon he cut all the limbs of the dead one loose and threw them into the water, made a fire under the kettle and let them boil.
sentences.i: Thereupon he cut all the dead girl’s limbs away and threw them into the water, made a fire under the kettle, and let them boil.
sentences.n: losschneiden is separable: schnitt … los. der Todten is the genitive of the adjective used as a noun, “of the dead one.” The tale reports the dismemberment as flatly as it reports the cooking, and nothing is softened.

sentences.t: Und wie alles Fleisch von den Knochen herabgefallen war, nahm er das schöne weiße Gebein heraus, und legte es auf eine Tafel, und reihte und legte es nach seiner natürlichen Ordnung zusammen.
sentences.l: And when all the flesh had fallen down from the bones, he took the fine white bone-work out, and laid it on a board, and ranged and laid it together according to its natural order.
sentences.i: And when all the flesh had fallen from the bones, he lifted out the fine white bones, laid them on a board, and set them together in their natural order.
sentences.n: Gebein is a collective — the whole frame of bones, singular in German where English needs a plural. herabfallen, herausnehmen and zusammenlegen are all separable, and their prefixes come to rest at the end of each clause. Tafel here is a board or slab, not a table laid for a meal.

sentences.t: Als das geschehen war, trat er davor und sprach dreimal „im Namen der allerheiligsten Dreifaltigkeit, Todte, steh auf.“
sentences.l: When that had happened, he stepped before it and said three times “in the name of the most holy Trinity, dead one, stand up.”
sentences.i: When that was done, he stepped in front of it and said three times, “In the name of the most holy Trinity, dead one, arise.”
sentences.n: Dreifaltigkeit is the Trinity, and the formula is a church one — the tale has a saint work by it. Todte is a vocative, addressing the dead girl. aufstehen is separable: steh … auf.

sentences.t: Und beim drittenmal erhob sich die Königstochter lebendig, gesund und schön.
sentences.l: And at the third time the king’s daughter raised herself up, alive, well and beautiful.
sentences.i: And at the third time the king’s daughter rose up alive, well and beautiful.

sentences.t: Nun war der König darüber in großer Freude, und sprach zum heil. Petrus „begehre deinen Lohn, und wenns mein halbes Königreich wäre, so will ich dirs geben.“
sentences.l: Now the king was in great joy over it, and said to Saint Peter “demand your reward, and if it were my half kingdom, then I will give it to you.”
sentences.i: Now the king was overjoyed at it and said to Saint Peter, “Name your reward, and if it were half my kingdom, I would give it to you.”
sentences.n: begehre is the imperative of begehren, an elevated word for demanding or desiring. wäre is the subjunctive of the unreal case, “even if it were.” wenns is wenn es and dirs is dir es.

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus aber antwortete „ich verlange nichts dafür.“
sentences.l: Saint Peter, however, answered “I demand nothing for it.”
sentences.i: But Saint Peter answered, “I ask nothing for it.”

sentences.t: „O, du Hans Narr!“ dachte der Bruder Lustig bei sich, stieß seinen Cameraden in die Seite und sprach „sei doch nicht so dumm, wenn du nichts willst, so brauch ich doch was.“
sentences.l: “Oh, you Jack Fool!” thought Brother Lustig with himself, poked his comrade in the side and said “do not be so stupid, if you want nothing, then I do need something.”
sentences.i: “Oh, you great simpleton!” thought Brother Lustig to himself; he jabbed his comrade in the ribs and said, “Do not be so stupid — if you want nothing, I want something.”
sentences.n: Hans Narr is a stock name for a fool, Hans being the everyman name of the tales. bei sich denken is “to think to oneself.” The two doch pull in opposite directions: the first presses a command, the second insists against what has just been said.

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus aber wollte nichts;
sentences.l: Saint Peter, however, wanted nothing;
sentences.i: But Saint Peter would have nothing;

sentences.t: doch weil der König sah daß der andere gerne was wollte, ließ er ihm vom Schatzmeister seinen Ranzen mit Gold anfüllen.
sentences.l: yet because the king saw that the other one gladly wanted something, he had his knapsack filled up with gold for him by the treasurer.
sentences.i: but as the king saw that the other man would gladly have something, he had the treasurer fill his knapsack with gold for him.
sentences.n: gerne with a verb of wanting means “would like to.” ließ … anfüllen is lassen plus infinitive for having a thing done, with vom Schatzmeister naming who does it, exactly as English uses “by.”

sentences.t: Sie zogen darauf weiter und wie sie in einen Wald kamen, sprach der heil. Petrus zum Bruder Lustig „jetzt wollen wir das Gold theilen.“
sentences.l: They moved on thereupon and when they came into a wood, Saint Peter said to Brother Lustig “now we will divide the gold.”
sentences.i: They went on after that, and when they came into a wood Saint Peter said to Brother Lustig, “Now let us divide the gold.”
sentences.n: wollen wir … is the ordinary German way of saying “let us.” theilen is the 1857 teilen.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ antwortete er, „das wollen wir thun.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” answered he, “that we will do.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” he answered, “let us do that.”

sentences.t: Da theilte der heil. Petrus das Gold, und theilte es in drei Theile.
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter divided the gold, and divided it into three parts.

sentences.t: Dachte der Bruder Lustig „was er wieder für einen Sparren im Kopf hat! macht drei Theile, und unser sind zwei.“
sentences.l: Thought Brother Lustig “what a rafter he has again in his head! makes three parts, and of us there are two.”
sentences.i: Brother Lustig thought, “What a crazy notion he has taken into his head again! He makes three parts, and there are two of us.”
sentences.n: einen Sparren haben — to have a rafter loose in one’s head — is the idiom for being cracked, our “to have a screw loose”; the literal keeps the German picture. unser sind zwei is an old genitive, “of us there are two.” macht has no subject at all, as a running comment in speech often does not.

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus aber sprach „nun habe ich genau getheilt, ein Theil für mich, ein Theil für dich, und ein Theil für den, der das Herz vom Lamm gegessen hat.“
sentences.l: Saint Peter, however, said “now I have divided exactly, one part for me, one part for you, and one part for the one who has eaten the heart of the lamb.”
sentences.i: But Saint Peter said, “Now I have divided it exactly: one part for me, one part for you, and one part for whoever ate the lamb’s heart.”
sentences.n: für den, der … — the demonstrative den carries the relative clause, “for that one who.” The trap is set with a perfectly straight face.

sentences.t: „O, das hab ich gegessen,“ antwortete der Bruder Lustig und strich geschwind das Gold ein, „das kannst du mir glauben.“
sentences.l: “Oh, that I have eaten,” answered Brother Lustig and swept the gold in quickly, “that you can believe me.”
sentences.i: “Oh, I ate that,” answered Brother Lustig, and he swept the gold up quickly, “you may take my word for it.”
sentences.n: einstreichen is separable, “to rake in, pocket.” The object das stands first in both speeches, which is where German puts the thing at issue.

sentences.t: „Wie kann das wahr sein,“ sprach der heil. Petrus, „ein Lamm hat ja kein Herz.“
sentences.l: “How can that be true,” said Saint Peter, “a lamb has no heart, after all.”
sentences.i: “But how can that be true,” said Saint Peter, “when a lamb has no heart?”

sentences.t: „Ei was, Bruder, wo denkst du hin! ein Lamm hat ja ein Herz, so gut wie jedes Thier, warum sollte das allein keins haben?“
sentences.l: “Ah what, brother, where do you think to! a lamb has a heart of course, just as well as every animal, why should that one alone have none?”
sentences.i: “Nonsense, brother, what can you be thinking of! Of course a lamb has a heart, as much as any other animal — why should it alone have none?”
sentences.n: wo denkst du hin is the fixed exclamation “what can you be thinking of”; hindenken is separable, and the wo … hin frame splits around the clause. The soldier now argues the exact opposite of what he argued before, with the same little ja.

sentences.t: „Nun, es ist schon gut,“ sagte der heil. Petrus, „behalt das Gold allein, aber ich bleibe nicht mehr bei dir und will meinen Weg allein gehen.“
sentences.l: “Now, it is all right,” said Saint Peter, “keep the gold alone, but I stay no longer with you and will go my way alone.”
sentences.i: “Well, let it be,” said Saint Peter, “keep the gold for yourself, but I stay with you no longer and will go my own way.”
sentences.n: behalt is the imperative of behalten with no ending, as the tales print it. seinen Weg gehen takes the way travelled as an accusative object.

sentences.t: „Wie du willst, Bruderherz,“ antwortete der Soldat, „leb wohl.“
sentences.l: “As you will, brother-heart,” answered the soldier, “live well.”
sentences.i: “As you please, brother dear,” answered the soldier, “farewell.”
sentences.n: leb wohl is the old parting formula, literally “live well” — English farewell is built the same way.

sentences.t: Da gieng der heil. Petrus eine andere Straße, Bruder Lustig aber dachte „es ist gut, daß er abtrabt, es ist doch ein wunderlicher Heiliger.“
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter went another road, Brother Lustig, however, thought “it is good that he trots off, he is a strange saint after all.”
sentences.i: So Saint Peter took another road, but Brother Lustig thought, “It is just as well that he is trotting off; he is an odd sort of saint.”
sentences.n: eine andere Straße gehen takes the accusative — the road travelled is an object, not a place. abtraben is said of horses, so the soldier is being rude. wunderlicher Heiliger is a set expression for an odd fish, and the joke is that this one is a saint in fact.

sentences.t: Nun hatte er zwar Geld genug, wußte aber nicht mit umzugehen, verthats, verschenkts, und wie eine Zeit herum war, hatte er wieder nichts.
sentences.l: Now he had indeed money enough, but did not know how to deal with it, squandered it, gave it away, and when a while was round, he had nothing again.
sentences.i: Now he had money enough, to be sure, but he did not know how to handle it: he squandered it, gave it away, and when a while had gone round he had nothing again.
sentences.n: zwar … aber is the pair “to be sure … but.” mit umzugehen is short for mit ihm umzugehen, the pronoun dropped in speech; umgehen takes mit. verthats and verschenkts are verthat es and verschenkt es run together, and verthat is the 1857 vertat, from vertun, to squander. verthat is a past tense, but verschenkt is present in form — the tale slips into the vivid present for a moment, and English needs a past for both.

sentences.t: Da kam er in ein Land, wo er hörte daß die Königstochter gestorben wäre.
sentences.l: Then he came into a country where he heard that the king’s daughter had died.

sentences.t: „Holla,“ dachte er, „das kann gut werden, die will ich wieder lebendig machen, und mirs bezahlen lassen, daß es eine Art hat.“
sentences.l: “Hallo,” thought he, “that can turn out well, her I will make alive again, and have it paid me so that it has a manner.”
sentences.i: “Hallo,” he thought, “this could turn out well: I will bring her back to life and have myself paid for it in style.”
sentences.n: daß es eine Art hat is an old idiom, “so that it is something to see, properly, in style.” mirs bezahlen lassen is again lassen for having a thing done, with mir the dative of the person paid. die is the demonstrative for “her.”

sentences.t: Gieng also zum König und bot ihm an die Todte wieder zu erwecken.
sentences.l: Went therefore to the king and offered him to wake the dead one again.
sentences.i: So he went to the king and offered to raise the dead girl.
sentences.n: The sentence begins with no subject at all — er is simply dropped, a brisk narrative habit of the tales. anbieten is separable, bot … an, and takes zu with the infinitive.

sentences.t: Nun hatte der König gehört daß ein abgedankter Soldat herumziehe, und die Gestorbenen wieder lebendig mache, und dachte der Bruder Lustig wäre dieser Mann, doch, weil er kein Vertrauen zu ihm hatte, fragte er erst seine Räthe, die sagten aber er könnte es wagen, da seine Tochter doch todt wäre.
sentences.l: Now the king had heard that a discharged soldier was travelling about, and making the dead alive again, and thought Brother Lustig was this man, yet, because he had no trust in him, he first asked his councillors, but they said he could risk it, since his daughter was dead anyway.
sentences.i: Now the king had heard that a discharged soldier was going about the country making the dead live again, and he thought Brother Lustig was this man; but as he had no confidence in him he asked his councillors first, and they said he might well risk it, since his daughter was dead in any case.
sentences.n: Five verb forms in a row are subjunctive — herumziehe, mache, wäre, könnte, wäre — holding the whole sentence at one remove: this is what the king heard and what the councillors said, not what the tale asserts. Räthe is the 1857 Räte, the king’s councillors.

sentences.t: Nun ließ sich der Bruder Lustig Wasser im Kessel bringen, hieß jedermann hinausgehen, schnitt die Glieder ab, warf sie ins Wasser und machte Feuer darunter, gerade wie er es beim heil. Petrus gesehen hatte.
sentences.l: Now Brother Lustig had water brought to himself in the kettle, bade everyone go out, cut the limbs off, threw them into the water and made a fire under it, just as he had seen it with Saint Peter.
sentences.i: Now Brother Lustig had water brought in the kettle, bade everyone go out, cut off the limbs, threw them into the water and made a fire under it, exactly as he had seen Saint Peter do.
sentences.n: ließ sich … bringen is lassen for having something done, with the dative reflexive sich for his own benefit. abschneiden is separable: schnitt … ab. darunter is a da- compound, “under it.”

sentences.t: Das Wasser fieng an zu kochen, und das Fleisch fiel herab, da nahm er das Gebein heraus und that es auf die Tafel;
sentences.l: The water began to boil, and the flesh fell down, then he took the bone-work out and put it on the board;
sentences.i: The water began to boil and the flesh fell away, so he took out the bones and put them on the board;
sentences.n: fieng is the 1857 fing; anfangen is separable and takes zu with the infinitive — fieng an zu kochen. that here is simply “put,” a use of thun still alive in spoken German.

sentences.t: er wußte aber nicht in welcher Ordnung es liegen mußte, und legte alles verkehrt durch einander.
sentences.l: but he did not know in what order it had to lie, and laid everything wrong through one another.
sentences.i: but he did not know in what order it had to lie, and put it all together the wrong way round.
sentences.n: durch einander, printed as two words here, is the modern durcheinander, in confusion. verkehrt is “the wrong way round.” es is the collective Gebein again, singular in German.

sentences.t: Dann stellte er sich davor, und sprach „im Namen der allerheiligsten Dreifaltigkeit, Todte, steh auf,“ und sprachs dreimal, aber die Gebeine rührten sich nicht.
sentences.l: Then he placed himself before it, and said “in the name of the most holy Trinity, dead one, stand up,” and said it three times, but the bones did not stir themselves.
sentences.i: Then he placed himself in front of it and said, “In the name of the most holy Trinity, dead one, arise,” and he said it three times, but the bones did not stir.
sentences.n: sich stellen and sich rühren are both reflexive, “to place oneself” and “to stir.” sprachs is sprach es. Here the plural die Gebeine is used where the earlier scene had the collective singular.

sentences.t: Da sprach er es noch dreimal, aber gleichfalls umsonst.
sentences.l: Then he said it three times more, but likewise in vain.
sentences.i: Then he said it three times more, but just as vainly.
sentences.n: umsonst means in vain here; the same word also means “for nothing, free of charge,” and only the sentence tells you which.

sentences.t: „Du Blitzmädel, steh auf,“ rief er, „steh auf, oder es geht dir nicht gut.“
sentences.l: “You lightning-girl, stand up,” cried he, “stand up, or it goes not well with you.”
sentences.i: “You confounded girl, get up,” he cried, “get up, or it will go badly for you.”
sentences.n: Blitzmädel, literally lightning-girl, is a rough soldier’s word of abuse. es geht dir nicht gut is impersonal with the dative, “things will not go well for you.” He is threatening a corpse, and the tale lets the blasphemy stand.

sentences.t: Wie er das gesprochen, kam der heil. Petrus auf einmal in seiner vorigen Gestalt, als verabschiedeter Soldat, durchs Fenster herein gegangen und sprach „du gottloser Mensch, was treibst du da, wie kann die Todte auferstehen, da du ihr Gebein so unter einander geworfen hast?“
sentences.l: When he had said that, Saint Peter came all at once in his former shape, as a discharged soldier, walking in through the window and said “you godless man, what are you carrying on there, how can the dead one rise again, since you have thrown her bones about among one another?”
sentences.i: When he had said that, Saint Peter came in all at once through the window in his former shape as a discharged soldier, and said, “You godless creature, what are you about? How can the dead girl rise again when you have thrown her bones together anyhow?”
sentences.n: gesprochen stands without its hatte — German drops the auxiliary in such subordinate clauses. herein gegangen kommen, “to come walking in,” is the German way of joining manner to motion. treiben here is “to be up to, carry on.” da at the head of the last clause is causal, “since.”

sentences.t: „Bruderherz, ich habs gemacht, so gut ich konnte“ antwortete er.
sentences.l: “Brother-heart, I have done it as well as I could,” answered he.
sentences.i: “Brother dear, I did it as well as I could,” he answered.
sentences.n: so gut ich konnte puts its verb at the end of the clause. habs is habe es. The flattering Bruderherz comes back the moment he is in trouble.

sentences.t: „Diesmal will ich dir aus der Noth helfen, aber das sag ich dir, wo du noch einmal so etwas unternimmst, so bist du unglücklich, auch darfst du von dem König nicht das Geringste dafür begehren oder annehmen.“
sentences.l: “This time I will help you out of the trouble, but this I tell you, where you undertake such a thing once more, then you are ruined, also you may not demand or accept the least thing from the king for it.”
sentences.i: “This time I will help you out of your trouble, but I tell you this: if ever you undertake such a thing again, you are done for; and you may not ask or accept the least thing from the king for it either.”
sentences.n: wo here means “if” — an old conditional use, not “where.” helfen takes the dative, dir. Noth is the 1857 Not. unglücklich in this older sense is stronger than unhappy: it is to be ruined. das Geringste is the superlative used as a noun, “the least thing.”

sentences.t: Darauf legte der heil. Petrus die Gebeine in ihre rechte Ordnung, sprach dreimal zu ihr „im Namen der allerheiligsten Dreifaltigkeit, Todte, steh auf,“ und die Königstochter stand auf, war gesund und schön wie vorher.
sentences.l: Thereupon Saint Peter laid the bones into their right order, said three times to her “in the name of the most holy Trinity, dead one, stand up,” and the king’s daughter stood up, was well and beautiful as before.
sentences.i: Thereupon Saint Peter laid the bones in their right order, said three times over her, “In the name of the most holy Trinity, dead one, arise,” and the king’s daughter stood up, sound and beautiful as before.
sentences.n: in ihre rechte Ordnung takes the accusative, because the bones are moved into that order. The formula comes back word for word, as it did the first time.

sentences.t: Nun gieng der heil. Petrus wieder durchs Fenster hinaus: der Bruder Lustig war froh daß es so gut abgelaufen war, ärgerte sich aber doch daß er nichts dafür nehmen sollte.
sentences.l: Now Saint Peter went out again through the window: Brother Lustig was glad that it had run off so well, but was vexed all the same that he was to take nothing for it.
sentences.i: Now Saint Peter went out through the window again: Brother Lustig was glad it had turned out so well, but vexed all the same that he was to take nothing for it.
sentences.n: ablaufen, separable, means “to run off, turn out.” sich ärgern is reflexive, “to be annoyed.” sollte here does not moralise but reports the instruction laid on him.

sentences.t: „Ich möchte nur wissen,“ dachte er, „was der für Mucken im Kopf hat, denn was er mit der einen Hand gibt, das nimmt er mit der andern: da ist kein Verstand drin.“
sentences.l: “I should only like to know,” thought he, “what whims that one has in his head, for what he gives with the one hand, that he takes with the other: there is no sense in it.”
sentences.i: “I should like to know,” he thought, “what whims the man has in his head, for what he gives with one hand he takes with the other: there is no sense in it.”
sentences.n: Mucken are whims, freaks of temper, and Mucken im Kopf haben answers the earlier Sparren im Kopf. der is again the demonstrative used of a person, faintly disrespectful. drin is the shortened darin.

sentences.t: Nun bot der König dem Bruder Lustig an was er haben wollte, er durfte aber nichts nehmen, doch brachte er es durch Anspielung und Listigkeit dahin, daß ihm der König seinen Ranzen mit Gold füllen ließ, und damit zog er ab.
sentences.l: Now the king offered Brother Lustig what he wanted to have, but he was not allowed to take anything, yet he brought it by hinting and cunning so far that the king had his knapsack filled with gold, and with that he moved off.
sentences.i: Now the king offered Brother Lustig whatever he wished, but he was not permitted to take anything; still, by hints and cunning he brought it so far that the king had his knapsack filled with gold, and off he went with it.
sentences.n: es dahin bringen, daß … is the idiom “to manage matters so that.” Anspielung is a hint dropped rather than a thing spoken outright. abziehen is separable: zog … ab.

sentences.t: Als er hinaus kam, stand vor dem Thor der heil. Petrus, und sprach „schau, was du für ein Mensch bist, habe ich dir nicht verboten etwas zu nehmen, und nun hast du den Ranzen doch voll Gold.“
sentences.l: When he came out, Saint Peter stood before the gate, and said “look, what sort of man you are, have I not forbidden you to take anything, and now you have the knapsack full of gold after all.”
sentences.i: When he came out, there stood Saint Peter before the gate, and he said, “Look at the sort of man you are: did I not forbid you to take anything, and now your knapsack is full of gold all the same.”
sentences.n: Thor is the 1857 Tor, a gate. was für ein is “what sort of.” verbieten takes the dative of the person forbidden and zu with the infinitive. voll Gold stands with no article and no preposition, the older construction.

sentences.t: „Was kann ich dafür,“ antwortete Bruder Lustig, „wenn mirs hinein gesteckt wird.“
sentences.l: “What can I do about it,” answered Brother Lustig, “if it is stuck in on me.”
sentences.i: “How am I to help it,” answered Brother Lustig, “if the gold is put in for me.”
sentences.n: für etwas können is the fixed idiom “to be to blame for something” — was kann ich dafür means “it is not my fault.” The passive gesteckt wird with the dative mir keeps every actor out of the sentence, which is exactly his defence.

sentences.t: „Das sag ich dir, daß du nicht zum zweitenmal solche Dinge unternimmst, sonst soll es dir schlimm ergehen.“
sentences.l: “This I tell you, that you do not undertake such things a second time, otherwise it shall go badly for you.”
sentences.i: “I tell you this: do not undertake such things a second time, or it shall go badly for you.”
sentences.n: The das points forward to the daß-clause that follows it. ergehen is impersonal with the dative: es ergeht dir schlimm, “you fare badly.”

sentences.t: „Ei, Bruder, sorg doch nicht, jetzt hab ich Gold, was soll ich mich da mit dem Knochenwaschen abgeben.“
sentences.l: “Ah, brother, do not worry, now I have gold, why should I trouble myself there with the bone-washing.”
sentences.i: “Ah, brother, do not fret; I have gold now — why should I bother with washing bones any more.”
sentences.n: sich abgeben mit is “to occupy oneself with, bother with.” Knochenwaschen, a compound made on the spot from an infinitive, is his cheerfully vulgar name for the miracle he has just watched. sorg is the short imperative of sorgen.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sprach der heil. Petrus, „das Gold wird lang dauern!
sentences.l: “Yes,” said Saint Peter, “the gold will last long!
sentences.i: “Oh yes,” said Saint Peter, “that gold will last a long while!
sentences.n: The line is ironic — Saint Peter means the opposite, as the next sentence makes plain. lang stands where modern German writes lange.

sentences.t: Damit du aber hernach nicht wieder auf unerlaubten Wegen gehst, so will ich deinem Ranzen die Kraft geben, daß alles, was du dir hinein wünschest, auch darin sein soll.
sentences.l: But so that you do not afterwards go on forbidden ways again, I will give your knapsack the power that everything you wish yourself in there shall also be in it.
sentences.i: But so that you do not take to forbidden ways again afterwards, I will give your knapsack the power that whatever you wish into it shall be there.
sentences.n: damit introduces a purpose, “so that,” and sends its verb to the end. dir with wünschest is a dative of advantage, “wish for yourself.” wünschest keeps the older full ending -est where modern German has -st.

sentences.t: Leb wohl, du siehst mich nun nicht wieder.“
sentences.l: Live well, you see me now no more.”
sentences.i: Farewell — you will not see me again.”
sentences.n: German uses the plain present siehst for the future; the time is carried by nun, not by the verb.

sentences.t: „Gott befohlen,“ sprach der Bruder Lustig, und dachte „ich bin froh daß du fortgehst, du wunderlicher Kauz, ich will dir wohl nicht nachgehen.“
sentences.l: “[Be] commended to God,” said Brother Lustig, and thought “I am glad that you are going away, you strange owl, I certainly will not go after you.”
sentences.i: “God keep you,” said Brother Lustig, and he thought, “I am glad you are going, you queer old bird; I shall not be running after you.”
sentences.n: Gott befohlen is a shortened old farewell, sei Gott befohlen, “be commended to God”; the literal supplies the missing verb in brackets. Kauz is a small owl and, of a person, an odd character — wunderlicher Kauz answers the earlier wunderlicher Heiliger. nachgehen is separable and takes the dative.

sentences.t: An die Wunderkraft aber, die seinem Ranzen verliehen war, dachte er nicht weiter.
sentences.l: Of the wonder-power, however, that had been bestowed on his knapsack, he thought no further.
sentences.i: But he thought no more about the miraculous power that had been given to his knapsack.
sentences.n: denken an takes the accusative, “to think of”; the an-phrase is pulled to the front of the sentence and dachte still stands second. verliehen war is the passive of verleihen, “to bestow.”

sentences.t: Bruder Lustig zog mit seinem Gold umher, und verthats und verfumfeits wie das erstemal.
sentences.l: Brother Lustig moved about with his gold, and squandered it and frittered it away as the first time.
sentences.i: Brother Lustig went about with his gold, and squandered it and frittered it away just as the first time.
sentences.n: verfumfeien is a rare colloquial verb for making away with something; that it means wasting is secure, and the pairing with verthats fixes it here, but how jocular or how coarse it sounded is a guess — the word is barely attested outside passages like this one. umherziehen is separable.

sentences.t: Als er nun nichts mehr als vier Kreuzer hatte, kam er an einem Wirthshaus vorbei und dachte „das Geld muß fort,“ und ließ sich für drei Kreuzer Wein und einen Kreuzer Brot geben.
sentences.l: When he now had nothing more than four Kreuzer, he came past an inn and thought “the money must away,” and had wine given him for three Kreuzer and bread for one Kreuzer.
sentences.i: When he had nothing left but four kreuzers, he came past an inn and thought, “The money must go,” and had them serve him three kreuzers’ worth of wine and one kreuzer’s worth of bread.
sentences.n: vorbeikommen is separable — kam … vorbei — and takes an with the dative for what one passes. das Geld muß fort has no verb of motion: muß carries it alone. Four kreuzers is exactly what he was discharged with, and the tale has come round to its beginning.

sentences.t: Wie er da saß und trank, kam ihm der Geruch von gebratenen Gänsen in die Nase.
sentences.l: As he sat there and drank, the smell of roasted geese came to him into the nose.
sentences.i: As he sat there drinking, the smell of roast geese came to his nose.

sentences.t: Bruder Lustig schaute und guckte, und sah daß der Wirth zwei Gänse in der Ofenröhre stehen hatte.
sentences.l: Brother Lustig looked and peered, and saw that the innkeeper had two geese standing in the oven.
sentences.i: Brother Lustig looked and peered about, and saw that the innkeeper had two geese standing in the oven.
sentences.n: stehen haben — haben with a bare infinitive of position — is the ordinary German way of saying that something is kept standing somewhere. Ofenröhre is the baking chamber of a stove.

sentences.t: Da fiel ihm ein daß ihm sein Camerad gesagt hatte was er sich in seinen Ranzen wünschte, das sollte darin sein.
sentences.l: Then it occurred to him that his comrade had said what he wished himself into his knapsack, that should be in it.
sentences.i: Then it came into his mind that his comrade had told him that whatever he wished into his knapsack should be there.
sentences.n: einfallen with the dative again — fiel ihm ein. The was-clause is picked up by das, the same doubling as before. sich wünschen is reflexive, “to wish for oneself.”

sentences.t: „Holla, das mußt du mit den Gänsen versuchen!“
sentences.l: “Hallo, that you must try with the geese!”
sentences.i: “Hallo — I must try that with the geese!”
sentences.n: He addresses himself as du, which German does freely in thought; the idiomatic English shifts to I, since English talks to itself in the first person.

sentences.t: Also gieng er hinaus, und vor der Thüre sprach er „so wünsch ich die zwei gebratenen Gänse aus der Ofenröhre in meinen Ranzen.“
sentences.l: So he went out, and before the door he said “so I wish the two roasted geese out of the oven into my knapsack.”
sentences.i: So he went out, and outside the door he said, “Now I wish the two roast geese out of the oven and into my knapsack.”
sentences.n: Thüre is the 1857 Türe. wünsch has lost its -e, as first persons and imperatives often do in the tales. The wish works by naming where the geese come from and where they go — aus with the dative, in with the accusative of motion.

sentences.t: Wie er das gesagt hatte, schnallte er ihn auf, und schaute hinein, da lagen sie beide darin.
sentences.l: When he had said that, he buckled it open, and looked in, and there they both lay inside.
sentences.i: When he had said that he unbuckled it and looked inside, and there the two of them lay.
sentences.n: aufschnallen is separable, “to unbuckle” — here the prefix auf undoes rather than fastens, as it does in aufmachen. hinein is motion inward, darin rest inside.

sentences.t: „Ach, so ists recht,“ sprach er, „nun bin ich ein gemachter Kerl,“ gieng fort auf eine Wiese und holte den Braten hervor.
sentences.l: “Ah, so it is right,” said he, “now I am a made fellow,” went off onto a meadow and fetched the roast out.
sentences.i: “Ah, that is the way,” he said, “now I am a made man,” and he went off to a meadow and brought out the roast.
sentences.n: ein gemachter Kerl uses the participle gemacht exactly as English uses it in “a made man.” hervorholen is separable, “to bring out.”

sentences.t: Wie er so im besten Essen war, kamen zwei Handwerksbursche daher und sahen die eine Gans, die noch nicht angerührt war, mit hungrigen Augen an.
sentences.l: As he was so in the best eating, two journeyman lads came along and looked at the one goose, which had not yet been touched, with hungry eyes.
sentences.i: While he was in the thick of his meal, two journeymen came along and eyed the goose that had not yet been touched with hungry eyes.
sentences.n: im besten Essen sein is the idiom for being in the middle of a meal. ansehen is separable, and its prefix waits to the very end of a long clause: sahen … an. Handwerksbursche are travelling journeymen, tramping from town to town for work — a familiar sight on the roads then.

sentences.t: Dachte der Bruder Lustig „mit einer hast du genug,“ rief die zwei Bursche herbei und sprach „da nehmt die Gans und verzehrt sie auf meine Gesundheit.“
sentences.l: Thought Brother Lustig “with one you have enough,” called the two lads over and said “there, take the goose and consume it to my health.”
sentences.i: Brother Lustig thought, “One is enough for you,” called the two lads over, and said, “Here, take the goose and eat it to my health.”
sentences.n: herbeirufen is separable, “to call over.” auf meine Gesundheit is the drinking formula, used here of eating. Again he speaks to himself as du.

sentences.t: Sie bedankten sich, giengen damit ins Wirthshaus, ließen sich eine Halbe Wein und ein Brot geben, packten die geschenkte Gans aus und fiengen an zu essen.
sentences.l: They thanked him, went with it into the inn, had a half of wine and a bread given them, packed the given goose out and began to eat.
sentences.i: They thanked him, went with it into the inn, had a half-measure of wine and a loaf brought, unwrapped the goose they had been given, and began to eat.
sentences.n: eine Halbe is a half-measure of wine with the measure-word left out, as one still orders “a half.” geschenkt is the participle of schenken used as an adjective, “given as a present.” auspacken is separable.

sentences.t: Die Wirthin sah zu und sprach zu ihrem Mann „die zwei essen eine Gans, sieh doch nach obs nicht eine von unsern aus der Ofenröhre ist.“
sentences.l: The innkeeper’s wife looked on and said to her husband “those two are eating a goose, do look after whether it is not one of ours out of the oven.”
sentences.i: The landlady watched and said to her husband, “Those two are eating a goose — go and see whether it is not one of ours from the oven.”
sentences.n: zusehen and nachsehen are both separable, “to look on” and “to go and check.” ob introduces an indirect question and sends its verb to the end. obs is ob es; von unsern uses the possessive as a noun, “of ours.”

sentences.t: Der Wirth lief hin, da war die Ofenröhre leer: „was, ihr Diebsgesindel, so wohlfeil wollt ihr Gänse essen! gleich bezahlt, oder ich will euch mit grünem Haselsaft waschen.“
sentences.l: The innkeeper ran over, and there the oven was empty: “what, you thieving rabble, so cheaply you want to eat geese! pay at once, or I will wash you with green hazel-juice.”
sentences.i: The innkeeper ran over, and there was the oven, empty: “What, you pack of thieves, do you mean to eat geese as cheap as that? Pay this instant, or I will wash you down with green hazel-juice.”
sentences.n: grüner Haselsaft, green hazel-juice, is a grim joke for a beating with a fresh hazel switch. Gesindel is rabble, and Diebsgesindel makes it thieving rabble. hinlaufen is separable, and gleich means “at once,” not “alike.”

sentences.t: Die zwei sprachen „wir sind keine Diebe, ein abgedankter Soldat hat uns die Gans draußen auf der Wiese geschenkt.“
sentences.l: The two said “we are no thieves, a discharged soldier gave us the goose out on the meadow.”
sentences.i: The two said, “We are no thieves — a discharged soldier made us a present of the goose out on the meadow.”

sentences.t: „Ihr sollt mir keine Nase drehen, der Soldat ist hier gewesen, aber als ein ehrlicher Kerl zur Thür hinaus gegangen, auf den hab ich Acht gehabt: ihr seid die Diebe und sollt bezahlen.“
sentences.l: “You shall not twist me any nose, the soldier has been here, but went out at the door as an honest fellow, on him I have had heed: you are the thieves and shall pay.”
sentences.i: “You shall not make a fool of me: the soldier was here, but he went out of the door like an honest man — I kept my eye on him. You are the thieves, and you shall pay.”
sentences.n: einem eine Nase drehen is an old idiom for hoodwinking someone, making a fool of him; the literal keeps the German picture. Acht haben auf is “to keep watch on.” Thür is the 1857 Tür.

sentences.t: Da sie aber nicht bezahlen konnten, nahm er den Stock und prügelte sie zur Thüre hinaus.
sentences.l: But since they could not pay, he took the stick and thrashed them out at the door.
sentences.i: But as they could not pay, he took his stick and beat them out of the door.
sentences.n: da at the head of a clause is causal, “since,” not “there.” zur Thüre hinaus is “out through the door,” with hinaus carrying the motion.

sentences.t: Bruder Lustig gieng seiner Wege und kam an einen Ort, da stand ein prächtiges Schloß und nicht weit davon ein schlechtes Wirthshaus.
sentences.l: Brother Lustig went his ways and came to a place, there stood a splendid castle and not far from it a poor inn.
sentences.i: Brother Lustig went his way and came to a place where a splendid castle stood, and not far from it a poor inn.
sentences.n: seiner Wege gehen is an old genitive phrase, “to go on one’s way.” schlecht here has its older sense of plain, mean, poor in quality, not morally bad.

sentences.t: Er gieng in das Wirthshaus und bat um ein Nachtlager, aber der Wirth wies ihn ab, und sprach „es ist kein Platz mehr da, das Haus ist voll vornehmer Gäste.“
sentences.l: He went into the inn and asked for a night’s lodging, but the innkeeper turned him away, and said “there is no room any more, the house is full of distinguished guests.”
sentences.i: He went into the inn and asked for a night’s lodging, but the innkeeper turned him away and said, “There is no room left; the house is full of gentlefolk.”
sentences.n: bitten um is “to ask for.” abweisen is separable: wies … ab. voll takes a bare genitive here, vornehmer Gäste, with no preposition.

sentences.t: „Das nimmt mich Wunder,“ sprach der Bruder Lustig, „daß sie zu euch kommen und nicht in das prächtige Schloß gehen.“
sentences.l: “That takes me wonder,” said Brother Lustig, “that they come to you and do not go into the splendid castle.”
sentences.i: “That surprises me,” said Brother Lustig, “that they come to you and do not go into the splendid castle.”
sentences.n: es nimmt mich Wunder is the old idiom for “it surprises me”; modern German says es wundert mich. euch is the plural you used to a stranger, as was usual then.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ antwortete der Wirth, „es hat was an sich, dort eine Nacht zu liegen, wers noch versucht hat, ist nicht lebendig wieder heraus gekommen.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” answered the innkeeper, “it has something about it to lie a night there, whoever has yet tried it has not come out again alive.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” answered the innkeeper, “there is something about lying a night there: whoever has tried it so far has not come out again alive.”
sentences.n: es hat was an sich means there is something about it, something uncanny. wers is wer es, and wer alone means “whoever.” noch here is “so far, ever yet.”

sentences.t: „Wenns andere versucht haben,“ sagte der Bruder Lustig, „will ichs auch versuchen.“
sentences.l: “If others have tried it,” said Brother Lustig, “I will try it too.”
sentences.i: “If others have tried it,” said Brother Lustig, “then so will I.”

sentences.t: „Das laßt nur bleiben,“ sprach der Wirth, „es geht euch an den Hals.“
sentences.l: “Just let that be,” said the innkeeper, “it goes you at the neck.”
sentences.i: “Better let that alone,” said the innkeeper, “it will cost you your neck.”
