sentences.n: etwas bleiben lassen is “to leave a thing alone, not do it.” an den Hals gehen is the idiom for what costs a man his life; the literal keeps the German picture and the idiomatic gives the sense.

sentences.t: „Es wird nicht gleich an den Hals gehen,“ sagte der Bruder Lustig, „gebt mir nur die Schlüssel und brav Essen und Trinken mit.“
sentences.l: “It will not go at the neck straight away,” said Brother Lustig, “just give me the keys and plenty of food and drink with them.”
sentences.i: “It will not come to my neck as quickly as that,” said Brother Lustig, “only give me the keys, and a good supply of food and drink with them.”
sentences.n: gleich here is “straight away.” brav in its older sense is “a good deal, plenty,” not “well-behaved.” Essen and Trinken are infinitives used as nouns.

sentences.t: Nun gab ihm der Wirth die Schlüssel und Essen und Trinken, und damit gieng der Bruder Lustig ins Schloß, ließ sichs gut schmecken, und als er endlich schläfrig wurde, legte er sich auf die Erde, denn es war kein Bett da.
sentences.l: Now the innkeeper gave him the keys and food and drink, and with that Brother Lustig went into the castle, let it taste good to himself, and when he at last grew sleepy, laid himself on the ground, for there was no bed there.
sentences.i: So the innkeeper gave him the keys and food and drink, and with that Brother Lustig went into the castle, made a hearty meal, and when he grew sleepy at last he lay down on the ground, for there was no bed.
sentences.n: sich etwas gut schmecken lassen is the set phrase for eating with relish; sichs is sich es. sich legen is reflexive, “to lay oneself down.” denn joins two main clauses and leaves the verb in second place, unlike weil.

sentences.t: Er schlief auch bald ein, in der Nacht aber wurde er von einem großen Lärm aufgeweckt, und wie er sich ermunterte, sah er neun häßliche Teufel in dem Zimmer, die hatten einen Kreiß um ihn gemacht und tanzten um ihn herum.
sentences.l: He fell asleep soon too, in the night, however, he was woken by a great noise, and when he roused himself, he saw nine hideous devils in the room, they had made a ring around him and danced around him.
sentences.i: He soon fell asleep, but in the night he was woken by a great din, and when he roused himself he saw nine hideous devils in the room; they had made a ring round him and were dancing about him.
sentences.n: einschlafen is separable, “to fall asleep.” aufgeweckt is the passive participle of aufwecken, with von naming what did the waking. sich ermuntern is reflexive, “to rouse oneself.” Kreiß is the 1857 spelling of Kreis, a ring, and the demonstrative die opens the last clause where English says “they.”

sentences.t: Sprach der Bruder Lustig „nun tanzt, so lang ihr wollt, aber komm mir keiner zu nah.“
sentences.l: Said Brother Lustig “now dance as long as you want, but let none come too near me.”
sentences.i: Brother Lustig said, “Dance as long as you like, but let none of you come too near me.”
sentences.n: komm … keiner is a third-person imperative with keiner as its subject, which English can only render with “let none of you come.” mir is the dative of the person the nearness concerns.

sentences.t: Die Teufel aber drangen immer näher auf ihn ein und traten ihm mit ihren garstigen Füßen fast ins Gesicht.
sentences.l: The devils, however, pressed ever nearer in upon him and trod him with their nasty feet almost into the face.
sentences.i: But the devils pressed nearer and nearer upon him and all but trod on his face with their filthy feet.
sentences.n: eindringen auf is separable, “to press in upon.” ihm … ins Gesicht is the dative of the person once more: German treads to him into the face, English treads on his face.

sentences.t: „Habt Ruh, ihr Teufelsgespenster,“ sprach er, aber sie triebens immer ärger.
sentences.l: “Have peace, you devil-spectres,” said he, but they drove it ever worse.
sentences.i: “Give over, you devilish spectres,” he said, but they carried on worse and worse.
sentences.n: Ruh is the shortened Ruhe. es treiben is “to carry on, behave,” and triebens is trieben es. immer with a comparative again means “more and more.”

sentences.t: Da ward der Bruder Lustig bös und rief „holla, ich will bald Ruhe stiften!“ kriegte ein Stuhlbein und schlug mitten hinein.
sentences.l: Then Brother Lustig became angry and cried “hallo, I will soon establish quiet!” got hold of a chair-leg and struck right into the middle.
sentences.i: Then Brother Lustig grew angry and cried, “Hallo there, I shall soon make peace here!” and he got hold of a chair-leg and struck right into the middle of them.
sentences.n: ward again for wurde, here with an adjective: “became angry.” Ruhe stiften is to establish quiet, restore order. mitten hinein, “right into the midst.”

sentences.t: Aber neun Teufel gegen einen Soldaten war doch zu viel, und wenn er auf den vordern zuschlug, so packten ihn die andern hinten bei den Haaren und rissen ihn erbärmlich.
sentences.l: But nine devils against one soldier was too much after all, and when he struck at the front ones, the others seized him behind by the hairs and tore at him pitifully.
sentences.i: But nine devils against one soldier was too much after all, and whenever he struck at the ones in front, the others seized him from behind by the hair and pulled him about pitifully.
sentences.n: wenn here is “whenever,” of a thing that happens again and again. zuschlagen is separable, “to strike out at.” German takes hold bei the part — bei den Haaren — with the article where English says “his.”

sentences.t: „Teufelspack,“ rief er, „jetzt wird mirs zu arg: wartet aber!
sentences.l: “Devil’s pack,” cried he, “now it is becoming too bad for me: but wait!
sentences.i: “You devil’s crew,” he cried, “now this is getting past bearing — but just wait!
sentences.n: mir wird es zu arg is the dative construction, “it is becoming too much for me.” Pack is a rabble or crew, always abusive.

sentences.t: Alle neune in meinen Ranzen hinein!“ husch, steckten sie darin, und nun schnallte er ihn zu und warf ihn in eine Ecke.
sentences.l: All nine into my knapsack in!” whisk, they were stuck inside, and now he buckled it shut and threw it into a corner.
sentences.i: All nine of you into my knapsack!” Whisk — there they were inside; and he buckled it up and threw it into a corner.
sentences.n: The wish has no verb at all: in meinen Ranzen hinein carries the whole of it. neune is the older full counting form of neun. husch is the word for a thing done in a flash. zuschnallen is separable, “to buckle shut.”

sentences.t: Da wars auf einmal still, und Bruder Lustig legte sich wieder hin und schlief bis an den hellen Morgen.
sentences.l: Then it was all at once still, and Brother Lustig laid himself down again and slept until the bright morning.
sentences.i: Then all at once it was quiet, and Brother Lustig lay down again and slept till broad morning.
sentences.n: wars is war es. sich hinlegen is separable and reflexive, “to lie down.” bis an den hellen Morgen is “right into broad daylight.”

sentences.t: Nun kamen der Wirth und der Edelmann, dem das Schloß gehörte, und wollten sehen wie es ihm ergangen wäre;
sentences.l: Now the innkeeper came and the nobleman to whom the castle belonged, and they wanted to see how it had gone with him;
sentences.i: Now the innkeeper came, and the nobleman the castle belonged to, and they wanted to see how he had fared;
sentences.n: dem is the relative pronoun in the dative, because gehören takes the dative. ergangen wäre is the impersonal ergehen again, in the subjunctive because it is the content of what they wanted to learn.

sentences.t: als sie ihn gesund und munter erblickten, erstaunten sie und fragten „haben euch denn die Geister nichts gethan?“
sentences.l: when they caught sight of him well and lively, they were astonished and asked “have the spirits then done you nothing?”
sentences.i: when they caught sight of him sound and lively they were astonished, and asked, “Did the spirits do you no harm, then?”
sentences.n: erblicken is a step above sehen, “to catch sight of.” gethan is the 1857 getan. euch is again the plural you of polite address, here in the dative.

sentences.t: „Warum nicht gar,“ antwortete Bruder Lustig, „ich habe sie alle neune in meinem Ranzen.
sentences.l: “Why not indeed,” answered Brother Lustig, “I have all nine of them in my knapsack.
sentences.i: “Nothing of the kind,” answered Brother Lustig, “I have all nine of them in my knapsack.
sentences.n: warum nicht gar is a fixed exclamation of scornful denial, roughly “what an idea, nothing of the sort” — it is not the question it looks like.

sentences.t: Ihr könnt euer Schloß wieder ganz ruhig bewohnen, es wird von nun an keiner mehr darin umgehen!“
sentences.l: You can inhabit your castle again quite peacefully, from now on none will walk in it any more!”
sentences.i: You may live in your castle again in perfect peace: from now on not one of them will haunt it any more!”
sentences.n: umgehen said of spirits means to walk or haunt — the same verb that meant “to handle” when it had mit with it, which is why a German verb must always be read together with its preposition. von nun an is “from now on.”

sentences.t: Da dankte ihm der Edelmann, beschenkte ihn reichlich und bat ihn in seinen Diensten zu bleiben, er wollte ihn auf sein Lebtag versorgen.
sentences.l: Then the nobleman thanked him, made him rich presents and asked him to stay in his services, he would provide for him for his lifetime.
sentences.i: Then the nobleman thanked him, made him handsome presents, and begged him to stay in his service; he would keep him for the rest of his life.
sentences.n: danken takes the dative, ihm. beschenken takes the person as its object — one be-gifts the man, not the gift. auf sein Lebtag is the old phrase for a whole lifetime. The last clause is his offer, reported without daß.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete er, „ich bin an das Herumwandern gewöhnt, ich will weiter ziehen.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered he, “I am accustomed to the wandering about, I will move on further.”
sentences.i: “No,” he answered, “I am used to wandering about; I will move on.”
sentences.n: an etwas gewöhnt sein is “to be used to something,” with the accusative after an. Herumwandern is another infinitive turned into a noun.

sentences.t: Da gieng der Bruder Lustig fort, trat in eine Schmiede und legte den Ranzen, worin die neun Teufel waren, auf den Ambos, und bat den Schmied und seine Gesellen zuzuschlagen.
sentences.l: Then Brother Lustig went off, stepped into a smithy and laid the knapsack, in which the nine devils were, on the anvil, and asked the smith and his journeymen to strike away.
sentences.i: Then Brother Lustig went off, stepped into a smithy, laid the knapsack with the nine devils in it on the anvil, and asked the smith and his men to strike.
sentences.n: worin is “in which,” a wo- compound used for things instead of in dem. Ambos is the 1857 spelling of Amboß. Gesellen are journeymen, trained men working under a master — the rank between apprentice and master in the guild.

sentences.t: Die schlugen mit ihren großen Hämmern aus allen Kräften zu, daß die Teufel ein erbärmliches Gekreisch erhoben.
sentences.l: They struck away with their great hammers out of all their strength, so that the devils raised a piteous screeching.
sentences.i: They struck away with their great hammers with all their might, so that the devils set up a piteous screeching.
sentences.n: Die at the head of the sentence is the demonstrative used for “they.” aus allen Kräften is “with all one’s might.” The Ge- prefix in Gekreisch makes a noun of continuous noise out of the verb kreischen, a very productive German pattern.

sentences.t: Wie er danach den Ranzen aufmachte, waren achte todt, einer aber, der in einer Falte gesessen hatte, war noch lebendig, schlüpfte heraus und fuhr wieder in die Hölle.
sentences.l: When he afterwards opened the knapsack, eight were dead, one, however, who had sat in a fold, was still alive, slipped out and went again into hell.
sentences.i: When he opened the knapsack afterwards, eight were dead; but one, who had been sitting in a fold of it, was still alive, slipped out, and went back to hell.
sentences.n: achte, like neune above, is the older counting form of acht. fahren is used of spirits moving swiftly, “to go, rush,” and it will come back at the end of the tale.

sentences.t: Darauf zog der Bruder Lustig noch lange in der Welt herum, und wers wüßte, könnte viel davon erzählen.
sentences.l: Thereupon Brother Lustig moved about in the world for a long time yet, and whoever knew it could tell much of it.
sentences.i: After that Brother Lustig wandered about the world for a long while yet, and whoever knew the story could tell a great deal of it.
sentences.n: wüßte and könnte are subjunctives of the unreal case, “if anyone knew it, he could tell.” wers is wer es. herumziehen is separable.

sentences.t: Endlich aber wurde er alt, und dachte an sein Ende, da gieng er zu einem Einsiedler, der als ein frommer Mann bekannt war und sprach zu ihm „ich bin das Wandern müde und will nun trachten in das Himmelreich zu kommen.“
sentences.l: At last, however, he grew old, and thought of his end, then he went to a hermit who was known as a pious man and said to him “I am weary of the wandering and will now strive to come into the kingdom of heaven.”
sentences.i: But at last he grew old and thought of his end, so he went to a hermit who was known for a pious man, and said to him, “I am weary of wandering and will now try to come into the kingdom of heaven.”
sentences.n: etwas müde sein, “to be weary of a thing,” took the genitive in older German, but here das Wandern stands unchanged — the tales are not strict about it. trachten takes zu with the infinitive, “to strive to.” An Einsiedler is one who lives apart, a hermit.

sentences.t: Der Einsiedler antwortete „es gibt zwei Wege, der eine ist breit und angenehm, und führt zur Hölle, der andere ist eng und rauh, und führt zum Himmel.“
sentences.l: The hermit answered “there are two ways, the one is broad and pleasant, and leads to hell, the other is narrow and rough, and leads to heaven.”
sentences.i: The hermit answered, “There are two roads: one is broad and pleasant and leads to hell, the other is narrow and rough and leads to heaven.”
sentences.n: es gibt with the accusative is the German for “there is, there are.” The two roads come from the Gospel image of the broad and the narrow way, which the hermit states as common knowledge.

sentences.t: „Da müßt ich ein Narr sein,“ dachte der Bruder Lustig, „wenn ich den engen und rauhen Weg gehen sollte.“
sentences.l: “There I should have to be a fool,” thought Brother Lustig, “if I were to go the narrow and rough way.”
sentences.i: “I should have to be a fool,” thought Brother Lustig, “to take the narrow and rough road.”
sentences.n: müßt is the clipped subjunctive müßte, and sollte is subjunctive too — both mark the case as unreal, “if I were to.”

sentences.t: Machte sich auf und gieng den breiten und angenehmen Weg, und kam endlich zu einem großen schwarzen Thor, und das war das Thor der Hölle.
sentences.l: Set himself up and went the broad and pleasant way, and came at last to a great black gate, and that was the gate of hell.
sentences.i: He set out and took the broad and pleasant road, and came at last to a great black gate, and that was the gate of hell.
sentences.n: The sentence has no subject at all — er is simply dropped again, as it was when he went to the king. sich aufmachen is separable and reflexive, “to set out.”

sentences.t: Bruder Lustig klopfte an, und der Thorwächter guckte wer da wäre.
sentences.l: Brother Lustig knocked, and the gatekeeper looked [to see] who was there.
sentences.i: Brother Lustig knocked, and the gatekeeper peered out to see who was there.
sentences.n: anklopfen is separable, “to knock at a door.” guckte governs the question directly in German, so the literal supplies [to see] in brackets, which English cannot do without. wäre is the subjunctive of the indirect question.

sentences.t: Wie er aber den Bruder Lustig sah, erschrack er, denn er war gerade der neunte Teufel, der mit in dem Ranzen gesteckt hatte und mit einem blauen Auge davon gekommen war.
sentences.l: But when he saw Brother Lustig, he took fright, for he was precisely the ninth devil who had been stuck in the knapsack along with the rest and had come off with a blue eye.
sentences.i: But when he saw Brother Lustig he took fright, for he was the very ninth devil who had been shut in the knapsack with the others and had got off with a black eye.
sentences.n: erschrack is the 1857 form of erschrak, from erschrecken, to take fright. mit … gesteckt hatte means stuck in along with the others. mit einem blauen Auge davonkommen is the fixed idiom for escaping lightly — German says a blue eye where English says a black one.

sentences.t: Darum schob er den Riegel geschwind wieder vor, lief zum Obersten der Teufel, und sprach „draußen ist ein Kerl mit einem Ranzen und will herein, aber laßt ihn bei Leibe nicht herein, er wünscht sonst die ganze Hölle in seinen Ranzen.
sentences.l: Therefore he pushed the bolt quickly to again, ran to the chief of the devils, and said “outside there is a fellow with a knapsack and wants in, but on no account let him in, otherwise he wishes the whole of hell into his knapsack.
sentences.i: So he pushed the bolt to again quickly, ran to the chief of the devils, and said, “There is a fellow outside with a knapsack who wants to come in, but on your life do not let him in, or he will wish the whole of hell into his knapsack.
sentences.n: vorschieben is separable, of shooting a bolt across. bei Leibe nicht, literally “not by your body,” is the old strong prohibition, on no account. will herein again has no verb of motion — wollen carries it. sonst is “otherwise, or else.”

sentences.t: Er hat mich einmal garstig darin hämmern lassen.“
sentences.l: He once had me hammered nastily in there.”
sentences.i: He once had me hammered inside it, and cruelly.”
sentences.n: lassen with a bare infinitive yet again, “had me hammered.” garstig is nasty, ugly, here of the treatment. The devil’s complaint is the tale’s last word on the smithy.

sentences.t: Also ward dem Bruder Lustig hinaus gerufen er sollte wieder abgehen, er käme nicht herein.
sentences.l: So it was called out to Brother Lustig he should go away again, he would not come in.
sentences.i: So word was called out to Brother Lustig that he was to be off again, and that he was not coming in.
sentences.n: ward … gerufen is an impersonal passive with no subject at all, which German can build where English must supply “it” or “word.” sollte and käme are the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: „Wenn sie mich da nicht wollen,“ dachte er, „will ich sehen ob ich im Himmel ein Unterkommen finde, irgendwo muß ich doch bleiben.“
sentences.l: “If they do not want me there,” thought he, “I will see whether I find a lodging in heaven, somewhere I must stay after all.”
sentences.i: “If they will not have me there,” he thought, “I will see whether I can find a lodging in heaven; I must stay somewhere.”
sentences.n: wollen with a plain object means “to want someone.” ob introduces the indirect question and sends its verb to the end. Unterkommen, another noun made from an infinitive, is a place where one is taken in.

sentences.t: Kehrte also um und zog weiter, bis er vor das Himmelsthor kam, wo er auch anklopfte.
sentences.l: Turned about therefore and moved on, until he came before the gate of heaven, where he also knocked.
sentences.i: So he turned about and went on until he came to the gate of heaven, where he knocked as well.
sentences.n: Another subjectless opening, and umkehren is separable: kehrte … um, “turned about.”

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus saß gerade dabei als Thorwächter: der Bruder Lustig erkannte ihn gleich und dachte „hier findest du einen alten Freund, da wirds besser gehen.“
sentences.l: Saint Peter sat just by it as gatekeeper: Brother Lustig recognised him at once and thought “here you find an old friend, here it will go better.”
sentences.i: Saint Peter happened to be sitting there as gatekeeper: Brother Lustig knew him at once and thought, “Here you have an old friend — things will go better here.”
sentences.n: gerade means “just, precisely,” of a lucky coincidence, and dabei is “by it.” He talks to himself as du once more. wirds is wird es, with the impersonal es geht, “things go.”

sentences.t: Aber der heil. Petrus sprach „ich glaube gar, du willst in den Himmel?“
sentences.l: But Saint Peter said “I really believe you want into heaven?”
sentences.i: But Saint Peter said, “I do believe you want to get into heaven?”
sentences.n: gar strengthens the verb, “actually, really.” willst in den Himmel is wollen alone again for wanting to go somewhere. The question is put as a statement with a question mark, as in speech.

sentences.t: „Laß mich doch ein, Bruder, ich muß doch wo einkehren; hätten sie mich in der Hölle aufgenommen, so wär ich nicht hierher gegangen.“
sentences.l: “Do let me in, brother, I must put up somewhere after all; had they in hell taken me in, then I would not have gone hither.”
sentences.i: “Do let me in, brother, I must put up somewhere; if they had taken me in down in hell, I would not have come here.”
sentences.n: einlassen is separable: laß … ein. einkehren is what a traveller does at an inn, to turn in for the night — he speaks of heaven as lodgings. hätten sie … is a conditional without wenn, made by putting the verb first, with the subjunctive for what did not happen. wo here is short for irgendwo.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sagte der heil. Petrus, „du kommst nicht herein.“
sentences.l: “No,” said Saint Peter, “you are not coming in.”

sentences.t: „Nun, willst du mich nicht einlassen, so nimm auch deinen Ranzen wieder: dann will ich gar nichts von dir haben,“ sprach der Bruder Lustig.
sentences.l: “Now, will you not let me in, then take your knapsack back too: then I will have nothing at all from you,” said Brother Lustig.
sentences.i: “Well, if you will not let me in, then take back your knapsack too: then I want nothing at all from you,” said Brother Lustig.
sentences.n: willst du … with the verb first is a conditional without wenn, “if you will not.” The knapsack is called Saint Peter’s because he gave it its power, and this is the hinge on which the whole ending turns.

sentences.t: „So gib ihn her’ sagte der heil. Petrus.
sentences.l: “Then give it here,” said Saint Peter.
sentences.i: “Hand it over, then,” said Saint Peter.
sentences.n: hergeben is separable, “to hand over,” with her marking motion toward the speaker. The speech is closed in our text by a stray ’ where the German closing mark belongs; whether the slip is the 1857 printer’s or the transcription’s cannot be settled from here, so it stands exactly as received and is flagged rather than corrected.

sentences.t: Da reichte er den Ranzen durchs Gitter in den Himmel hinein, und der heil. Petrus nahm ihn und hieng ihn neben seinen Sessel auf.
sentences.l: Then he passed the knapsack in through the grating into heaven, and Saint Peter took it and hung it up beside his seat.
sentences.i: Then he passed the knapsack in through the grating into heaven, and Saint Peter took it and hung it up beside his chair.
sentences.n: hieng is the 1857 spelling of hing, from aufhängen, which is separable: hieng … auf. durchs is durch das. The gate of heaven has a grating, like the gate of a town.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Bruder Lustig „nun wünsch ich mich selbst in meinen Ranzen hinein.“
sentences.l: Then Brother Lustig said “now I wish my own self into my knapsack.”
sentences.i: Then Brother Lustig said, “Now I wish myself into my knapsack.”
sentences.n: sich wünschen with a place named after it: the reflexive mich is what is wished in, and selbst underlines it — his own self and nothing else. The trick works because the knapsack is now inside heaven.

sentences.t: Husch, war er darin, und saß nun im Himmel, und der heil. Petrus mußte ihn darin lassen.
sentences.l: Whisk, he was inside it, and now sat in heaven, and Saint Peter had to let him stay in it.
sentences.i: Whisk — there he was inside, and now he sat in heaven, and Saint Peter had to let him stay.
sentences.n: husch comes back from the scene with the devils and closes the tale with the same trick. darin lassen is “to leave him in it” — the saint is beaten by his own gift, and the tale ends without a word of judgment.
